newsitem.title: USA: N.Y. official seeks U.S. monitors for Swiss banks.
newsitem.headline: N.Y. official seeks U.S. monitors for Swiss banks.

text.p: New York City's chief financial officer proposed on Wednesday that an ad hoc group of U.S. public officials should monitor how Swiss banks handle allegations that they kept the unclaimed wealth of Holocaust victims.
"I think it will be useful to exchange this information," Comptroller Alan Hevesi said at a news conference.

"We're not interested in applying pressure, we're interested in encouraging the Swiss to continue on a path that is positive," Hevesi said a week after a trip to Switzerland where he met Swiss banking and government officials and Jewish leaders.
Saying a coordinated approach was needed, Hevesi added: "We will be monitoring this and our relationship will be a function of their producing what they promised."

While he said whether Swiss banks are allowed to keep doing "substantial" business with the city depended on how they treat Holocaust victims, Hevesi stopped short of threatening punitive steps. "We're not ready to participate in a boycott. We want to encourage the Swiss to do the right thing."

Hevesi is a trustee and investment adviser for the city's $70 billion pension fund, which owned 322,880 shares -- a $47.6 million stake -- in the three major Swiss banks, as of Dec. 31, 1996. The banks also handle some of the city's short-term deposits.
Hevesi said he might contact state comptrollers and private pension funds as part of his effort to set up an ad hoc monitoring group.
Hevesi added that the Solidarity Fund for victims of poverty, disasters and oppression proposed by the Swiss government might never be enacted.
"The fund must be approved by a referendum, and virtually every government official, community leader and banker I spoke to thought that approval would be difficult."
